q.q: What is the central task of every software project, whatever methodology is used?
o: Deliver the software as quickly as possible by removing constraints and avoiding all risks
Meet the project objectives by deploying resources within the constraints while managing the risks
Use as many resources as are available so that no risk can ever cause the project to fail
Complete each stage of the waterfall model in order before the client signs off the scope
q.why: The notes define the central task as meeting objectives by deploying resources within constraints while managing risks, whether the method is waterfall, RAD or Agile.

q.q: Which of these is a technical resource on a software project?
o: A development server
A database administrator
The project budget
A meeting room
q.why: Technical resources include processing power, bandwidth, development servers and licences. A database administrator is a human resource and a meeting room is physical.

q.q: Software licences used by the development team are classified as which type of resource?
o: Technical
Financial
Physical
Human
q.why: Software licences are listed with processing power and bandwidth as technical resources, even though they cost money.

q.q: A resource that is used up over time, such as the project's money, is described as...
o: recurring
depleting
inelastic
dedicated
q.why: Depleting resources run down as they are used, e.g. money and time. Recurring resources, such as dedicated staff, do not run down.

q.q: A graphic designer works on this project and on two other projects at the same time. In terms of ownership, the designer is...
o: shared
dedicated
movable
inelastic
q.why: Ownership is dedicated (only this project) or shared (also used by other projects); the notes use a graphic designer as the shared example.

q.q: A company's server room cannot readily be moved to where it is needed. Which classification describes it?
o: Fixed
Inelastic
Depleting
Dedicated
q.why: Location is classified as fixed or movable; a server room is fixed. Inelastic refers to an amount that cannot be changed, which is a different property.

q.q: The project budget can be increased if the client agrees. Which property does this show?
o: It is recurring
It is movable
It is dedicated
It is elastic
q.why: Elastic resources can be increased or decreased, such as budget or number of staff; time before a hard deadline is inelastic.

q.q: During which resource-management activity are resources allocated to tasks and moved if a stage falls behind?
o: Planning
Deployment
Release
Scheduling
q.why: Deployment happens during the project: resources are allocated, stages monitored and resources moved if a stage falls behind.

q.q: Why does the project manager record any over- or under-use of resources after each stage?
o: So that the client can be charged for idle staff time
So that unused resources can be kept for the next stage
So that the project deadline can be moved back
So that future resource estimates can be improved
q.why: In the release activity, actual use is compared with the plan and differences are recorded so future estimates improve.

q.q: What is a constraint in a software project?
o: Anything that could harm the project or cause it to fail
A resource whose amount can be increased or decreased
A restriction placed on the project that the developer cannot change
A task on the critical path that has zero float
q.why: A constraint is a restriction the developer cannot change. Something that could harm the project is a risk, not a constraint.

q.q: Which of these is a scope constraint?
o: The project must go live by 30 June
The budget must not exceed £80,000
The lead programmer may leave the company
The system must give a response within two seconds
q.why: Scope constraints are characteristics of the product fixed by the client, e.g. response time. The deadline is a time constraint and the budget a resource constraint.

q.q: Which constraint is stated explicitly enough for a project?
o: Delivered as soon as possible, at low cost
Live by 30 June, maximum budget £80,000
Live in early summer, budget kept reasonable
Completed quickly and as cheaply as possible
q.why: Constraints must be explicit; phrases such as 'as soon as possible' can be read in many ways, but a date and a figure cannot.

q.q: Before signing off the scope, what must the project manager check about the time constraint?
o: That the deadline is an elastic resource that can be extended
That the work can actually be done in the time available
That the client has agreed to a range of possible deadlines
That every task on the project has some float
q.why: The notes say the project manager must check, before signing off the scope, that the work can be done in the time available.

q.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes a constraint from a risk?
o: A deadline is a constraint; the possibility of missing it is a risk
A deadline is a risk; the possibility of missing it is a constraint
Deadlines and missing them are both examples of scope constraints
A deadline is a resource; the possibility of missing it is a constraint
q.why: The notes stress this exact distinction: the deadline is fixed (constraint); missing it is something that could happen (risk).

q.q: What usually causes requirements shift?
o: Too much testing during the implementation stage
Using change control on the agreed specification
Splitting long tasks into smaller timed sections
Too little user involvement in the analysis stage
q.why: Requirements shift is often caused by too little user involvement in analysis, so users' needs change later.

q.q: How is the risk of requirements shift best reduced?
o: Split long tasks into smaller sections, each with its own short deadline
Involve users fully in analysis, agree a specification and use change control
Use pair programming, code reviews and good documentation throughout
Build contingency time into a realistic schedule and monitor it regularly
q.why: Those three measures target requirements shift. The other options reduce productivity, staff turnover and time risks respectively.

q.q: A key developer leaves halfway through a project. Which risk-reduction measure would have limited the damage most?
o: A detailed Gantt chart with contingency time
Documentation, code reviews and pair programming
A fixed-price contract agreed with the client
A single target value for each objective
q.why: Staff turnover risk is reduced by collaboration, documentation, code reviews and pair programming, so knowledge is not held by one person.

q.q: On a fixed-price contract, why is a missed deadline a particular problem for the developer?
o: The client can increase the scope for free
The developer pays for the extra work needed
The budget becomes an inelastic resource
The project manager must be replaced
q.why: The notes say that on a fixed-price contract the developer pays for extra work, and both parties' reputations suffer.

q.q: In a risk register, risk A has likelihood 4 and impact 2; risk B has likelihood 2 and impact 5. Which should get attention first?
o: Risk A, with a score of 8
Risk B, with a score of 10
Risk A, because likelihood matters most
Neither, as both total 6 or 7
q.why: Scores are likelihood × impact: A = 8, B = 10, so B is the higher-scoring risk and gets attention and an owner first.

q.q: Why is it harder to judge progress on a software project than on a building project?
o: Software is intangible, so half-built software cannot be seen
Software projects never have fixed deadlines to measure against
Software uses routine methods that rarely change during a project
Building projects are usually bespoke, so progress is obvious
q.why: Software is intangible; a building visibly rises, so progress is obvious.

q.q: Why do experience and solutions transfer less well between software projects than between construction projects?
o: Software projects are usually bespoke
Software projects are always intangible to clients
Software projects never use the same tools
Software projects have no repeated tasks
q.why: On repetition, software is usually bespoke, whereas similar construction developments repeat so pitfalls are familiar.

q.q: Which is a difference between software projects and construction projects identified in the notes?
o: Software projects do not need a project manager
Construction projects are intangible and hard to monitor
Software projects repeat, so pitfalls are familiar
New technology may appear mid-project and prompt changes
q.why: Technology changes rapidly in software; routine construction methods such as wiring rarely change during a project.

q.q: For which outcome is the project manager accountable?
o: Writing the system specification from the fact-finding results
Writing, documenting and unit-testing the code to standards
Delivering on time, within budget and to the required quality
Carrying out acceptance testing on behalf of the end users
q.why: The project manager is accountable for time, budget and quality. Writing the specification is the systems analyst's job.

q.q: Which of these is a performance indicator for an objective?
o: Project manager
Gantt chart
Error rate
Risk register
q.why: Performance indicators are metrics such as time taken, error rate or user satisfaction.

q.q: Which three parts does each clear project objective need?
o: A statement, a budget and a named programmer for each task
A statement, performance indicators and a success value for each
A deadline, a risk score and a performance indicator for each
A statement, a Gantt chart and an acceptance test for each
q.why: The notes list a clear statement, performance indicators (metrics) and the value of each that counts as success.

q.q: An objective says success is 'a 10–20% increase in sales'. What is the problem?
o: A percentage cannot be used as a performance indicator
Each side may claim a different point in the range as success
The objective has no performance indicator to measure
A range is not measurable, so the objective is not SMART
q.why: A single target value should be used; with a range one side may claim success at 10% while the other expects 20%.

q.q: In SMART objectives as used in the CCEA textbook, what does 'A' stand for?
o: Agreed
Achievable
Accurate
Actionable
q.why: In the textbook A is Agreed: signed off by client and developer before development begins. Achievable is a common misconception.

q.q: An objective reads: 'Reduce booking errors by 30% within six months of go-live, signed off by both parties.' Which SMART element does 'within six months' provide?
o: Measurable
Specific
Timed
Realistic
q.why: T – Timed means the objective has a target date; 'within six months' provides that.

q.q: Which objective is the best example of a SMART objective?
o: Make the checkout process much faster and easier for all of our users
Cut average checkout time by between 20% and 40% as soon as possible
Cut average checkout time to 90 seconds by 1 March, agreed by both sides
Improve checkout so customers are happier, agreed by the project team
q.why: It is specific, measurable (90 seconds), agreed, realistic and timed. The others are vague, use a range or lack a date and metric.

q.q: Which team member investigates the current system and writes the system specification?
o: Designer
Project manager
Systems analyst
Technical author
q.why: The systems analyst gathers requirements by fact-finding and writes the system specification.

q.q: Which role writes, documents and unit-tests code following the design and coding standards?
o: Tester
Programmer
Designer
Systems analyst
q.why: The programmer/developer writes, documents and unit-tests the code. The tester writes test plans and records defects.

q.q: Which role writes test plans, carries out testing and reports defects to developers?
o: Tester
Programmer
Project manager
Client representative
q.why: Testers write test plans, test, record defects and report them to developers.

q.q: Who usually carries out acceptance testing?
o: The tester employed by the developer
The programmer who wrote the code
Client or end-user representatives
The systems analyst
q.why: Client/end-user representatives provide requirements, review deliverables and carry out acceptance testing.

q.q: A company needs user guides and help files for a new system. Which team member produces them?
o: Technical author
Systems analyst
Trainer
Designer
q.why: The technical author writes user guides, help files and technical documentation. A trainer prepares users for changeover.

q.q: On a larger project, which role designs and maintains the database?
o: Database administrator
Systems analyst
Infrastructure specialist
Technical author
q.why: The notes list the database administrator as an extra role on bigger projects for designing and maintaining the database.

q.q: In an Agile project, which roles take on much of the co-ordinating and client-facing work?
o: The systems analyst and the technical author
The Scrum master and the product owner
The tester and the database administrator
The trainer and the infrastructure specialist
q.why: In Agile, the Scrum master and product owner take on much of the co-ordinating and client-facing work.

q.q: Why do clearly defined roles help a software project team?
o: Tasks are not missed or duplicated and it is clear who owns each deliverable
Every team member can change the scope directly without asking anyone
Fewer people are needed because each role can do every job on the project
Testing is no longer needed because each person checks their own work
q.why: Clear roles avoid gaps and duplication, help allocation by skill, give clear communication routes and accountability.

q.q: What is a Gantt chart?
o: A network of nodes and arrows showing earliest and latest times
A graph of version nodes with arrows from parent to child version
A chart showing the remaining work in each sprint of a project
A horizontal bar chart showing each task as a bar against a timeline
q.why: A Gantt chart is a horizontal bar chart of tasks against time. The network description is CPA; the last is a burn down chart.

q.q: Two bars on a Gantt chart overlap in time. What does this show?
o: The chart contains a scheduling error
One task depends on the other task
The tasks are scheduled to run in parallel
Both tasks are on the critical path
q.why: Overlapping bars are tasks carried out at the same time (in parallel).

q.q: Task F depends on task D, which finishes on day 12, and task E, which finishes on day 11. When is the earliest that F can start?
o: Day 11
Day 13
Day 23
Day 12
q.why: A task starts when the latest of its predecessors finishes, so F waits for D at day 12.

q.q: Task A (3 days) has no predecessors. Task B (4 days) depends on A. Task D (5 days) depends on B. What is the earliest finish of D?
o: Day 12
Day 9
Day 7
Day 5
q.why: A finishes at 3, B at 3 + 4 = 7, D at 7 + 5 = 12.

q.q: Task C (2 days) starts at day 3. Task G (2 days) depends only on C. When is the earliest G can finish?
o: Day 5
Day 4
Day 9
Day 7
q.why: C finishes at 3 + 2 = 5, so G runs from day 5 to day 7.

q.q: Task G finishes on day 7 but the task that depends on it, H, cannot start until day 15. How many days could G slip without delaying H?
o: 2 days
7 days
8 days
15 days
q.why: 15 − 7 = 8 days to spare, as in the notes' worked example.

q.q: What is the most common error when drawing a Gantt chart?
o: Drawing two bars that overlap in time on the same chart
Making the bar length equal to the duration of the task
Starting a bar before every task it depends on has finished
Showing a milestone at the end of a group of tasks
q.why: The notes highlight starting a bar before every predecessor has finished; overlap itself is normal and shows parallel tasks.

q.q: On a Gantt chart, a task has no spare time before the task that depends on it starts. How is this task described?
o: Parallel
Critical
Elastic
Depleting
q.why: Tasks with no spare time before their successor are critical: any delay delays the whole project.

q.q: Which of these can a project manager read from a Gantt chart?
o: The cost and quality of each task and of the whole project
When each task starts and finishes and which tasks overlap
The author, date and note for every change to the code
The likelihood and impact score of each project risk
q.why: A Gantt chart shows start, duration, end, overlap and dependencies (and milestones/progress). It does not show cost or quality.

q.q: In a critical path analysis network, what do the nodes (circles) represent?
o: Events, such as the end of one task and the start of the next
Tasks, labelled with their durations in days
Resources allocated to each task in the project
Versions of a file created from a parent version
q.why: Nodes are events; arrows are tasks labelled with durations.

q.q: In the forward pass, two arrows arrive at a node giving values of 9 and 12. What is the node's EST?
q.why: Take the highest value because every incoming task must be finished.

q.q: In the backward pass, two paths lead back to a node giving LFTs of 8 and 6. What is the node's LFT?
q.why: Take the lowest value so that neither later path is delayed.

q.q: How is the critical path identified on a completed CPA diagram?
o: It joins the nodes with the highest LFT values
It is the route containing the most tasks
It is the shortest route through the network
It joins the nodes where EST equals LFT
q.why: Critical nodes have no slack, so EST = LFT; the tasks joining them form the critical path.

q.q: Which statement about the critical path is correct?
o: It is the shortest route and gives the minimum project duration
It is the longest route and gives the minimum project duration
It is the route with the most float, so tasks can be delayed
It is the route through nodes with the lowest EST values
q.why: The critical path is always the longest route; it is the minimum time in which the whole project can be completed.

q.q: A task has EST 4 at its start node, LFT 13 at its end node and a duration of 6. What is its float?
q.why: Float = 13 − 4 − 6 = 3. A common slip is 13 − 4 = 9, forgetting the duration.

q.q: A task starts at a node with EST 5, ends at a node with LFT 12 and lasts 6 days. What is its float?
q.why: Float = 12 − 5 − 6 = 1 day, as for task E in the booking-system example.

q.q: A project has tasks A (3 days), B (4, after A), C (2, after A), D (5, after B), E (6, after C), F (3, after D and E). What is the earliest F can start?
q.why: Path A–B–D reaches 3 + 4 + 5 = 12; path A–C–E reaches 3 + 2 + 6 = 11. Take the highest, 12.

q.q: Tasks: A 3 days; B 4 days after A; C 2 days after A; D 5 after B; E 6 after C; F 3 after D and E; G 2 after C; H 1 after F and G. What is the critical path?
o: A, B, D, F, H
A, C, E, F, H
A, C, G, H
A, B, D, E, F, H
q.why: A–B–D–F–H totals 3 + 4 + 5 + 3 + 1 = 16, the longest route. A–C–E–F–H totals only 15.

q.q: In the forward pass, why is the highest value taken where several arrows meet at a node?
o: The highest value gives the most float to later tasks
It makes sure that no later path is delayed in the backward pass
Every incoming task must be finished before the next can start
The highest value is always on the shortest route
q.why: A node's event cannot occur until all incoming tasks are complete, so the latest (highest) arrival time is used.

q.q: During the backward pass, a node's next node has LFT 15 and the task leaving it lasts 3 days. What is the LFT at this node if there is only one path?
q.why: LFT = LFT of next node − duration of the task leaving = 15 − 3 = 12.

q.q: How do Gantt charts and CPA help reduce the overall duration of a project?
o: They remove the need to estimate task durations
They show the cost and quality of every task
They show which tasks can be carried out in parallel
They make all of the tasks in a project critical
q.why: Both tools identify parallel tasks, which reduces the overall project duration.

q.q: How do these tools help with resource planning?
o: Resources can be acquired at a task's LFT and released at its EST
Resources can be acquired at a task's EST and released at its LFT
The budget is calculated automatically from the critical path
Every resource is kept until the end of the whole project
q.why: Timing acquisition to the EST and release at the LFT means resources are not paid for while idle.

q.q: Which is an advantage of critical path analysis over a Gantt chart?
o: It is easier for the client to read and understand
It needs no estimates of how long tasks will take
It shows the cost of each task alongside its time
It identifies the critical path and float precisely
q.why: CPA calculates ESTs and LFTs, so critical tasks, float and minimum duration are explicit. Gantt charts are the easier ones for clients.

q.q: A manager wants a chart to show the client progress to date at a monthly meeting. Which tool is most suitable and why?
o: A Gantt chart, because it is easy to read and shows progress
A CPA network, because it shows the float of every task
A CPA network, because clients can see the critical path
A version graph, because it shows each change made so far
q.why: Gantt charts are best for day-to-day monitoring and reporting progress; CPA is harder to read and less suitable for clients.

q.q: A critical task slips by two days. Another task has five days of float. What can the manager do?
o: Move staff from the critical task onto the task with float to balance work
Move staff from the task with float onto the critical task to recover time
Ignore the delay, because the float on the other task absorbs it automatically
Delay the task with float by five days so that the two tasks run in parallel
q.why: Float on a non-critical task means staff can be moved from it onto the delayed critical task without delaying the project.

q.q: Which is a limitation of both Gantt charts and CPA?
o: They cannot show which tasks depend on others
They can only be drawn on paper by the manager
They only work for projects with a single task
They are only as accurate as the duration estimates
q.why: Both depend on duration estimates, which are often uncertain in software projects.

q.q: Why are Gantt charts and CPA less suited to Agile projects?
o: Agile scope changes sprint by sprint, so burn down charts are used instead
Agile projects have no tasks that depend on any other tasks at all
Agile teams are too large for a Gantt chart to show every member
Agile projects never have a deadline, so there is no critical path
q.why: The notes say both tools are less suited to Agile because scope changes sprint by sprint; burn down charts are used instead.

q.q: What is version management?
o: The process of making a backup copy of all project files every night
The process of deciding which version of the software to sell to clients
The process of numbering each release of the user guide and help files
The process by which a team keeps track of changes to its code files over time
q.why: Version management keeps track of changes to code files over time. The notes warn it is not simply saving files or making backups.

q.q: Which three things does a version management system record for each change?
o: Who made it, when, and a note describing it
Who made it, its cost, and its float
When it was made, its priority, and its risk score
Who approved it, the IP address, and the file size
q.why: Author, time and a descriptive note (including knock-on effects) are recorded with each new version.

q.q: In version management, where are all the project files held, with access monitored and every change tracked?
o: In a branch
In a data dictionary
In a repository
In a risk register
q.why: All files are held in a repository where access is monitored and every change tracked.

q.q: A new release introduces a serious bug. How does version management help?
o: The system finds and deletes the bug automatically
The deadline is extended until the bug is fixed
The team can return to a previous working version
Users are stopped from reporting the bug
q.why: Any earlier version can be retrieved, so the team can return to and develop from the last working version.

q.q: Two developers edit the same file at the same time. How does version management stop work being lost?
o: Only the most recent save is kept, so no clash occurs
The second developer is locked out of the project
Both versions are deleted and the file is restored
Changes are tracked and merged, and clashes are flagged
q.why: Changes are tracked and merged; clashes are flagged rather than one person's work silently overwriting the other's.

q.q: Why is version management especially important on large systems?
o: Many programmers share files, so unrestricted changes would cause chaos
Large systems do not need testing if version management is used
It removes the need for a project manager on large systems
It makes large programs run faster once they are released
q.why: With teams sharing a set of files, letting anyone change anything without restriction would quickly create chaos.

q.q: A developer's laptop fails. Why is no project history lost?
o: A remote repository holds a full copy of the history
The rollback feature restores the laptop's hard drive
Each commit is emailed to the project manager
Branches are stored in the laptop's memory
q.why: Hosted services keep a remote copy of the repository, so the history survives a local failure.

q.q: What does it mean to commit a change?
o: Combine two parallel versions into one version
Return to an earlier stable version of the code
Start a separate line of development for a feature
Save it as a new numbered version with a note
q.why: Committing creates a new numbered version. The other options describe merge, rollback and branch.

q.q: What is a branch?
o: A copy of the repository stored on a different site as a backup
A combined version containing two developers' sets of changes
An earlier stable version from which development continues
A separate line of development that does not disturb the main version
q.why: A branch lets a feature be built without disturbing the main version others rely on.

q.q: Two developers changed the same lines of a file in parallel versions. What happens when the versions are merged?
o: The later change automatically overwrites the earlier one
The merge is cancelled and both versions are deleted
The system flags a conflict for a person to resolve
The system rolls back to the version before both changes
q.why: If the same lines were changed, a conflict is flagged for a person to resolve.

q.q: What is a rollback?
o: Returning to an earlier stable version and continuing development from there
Combining an earlier stable version with the latest version of the file
Undoing the latest commit note but keeping all the code changes made
Copying the latest version to a remote repository as a safety backup
q.why: Rollback returns to an earlier stable version and continues from there, discarding the faulty changes.

q.q: On a version management graph, which way do arrows point?
o: From the newest version back to the version it replaced
From the main version to every branch that was merged in
From each developer's node to the version they edited
From the version a new one was created from to the new version
q.why: Arrows point from parent (older) to child (newer).

q.q: On a version management graph, two arrows enter one node. What does this show?
o: A rollback to an earlier version
Two developers branching in parallel
A version that was deleted
A merge of two parallel versions
q.why: Two incoming arrows mean two versions were combined into one.

q.q: A file has versions v1 to v5. v5 contains a fault, so the team rolls back to v4 and creates v6. Where does the arrow to v6 start?
o: v5
v1
v3
v4
q.why: v6 is developed from v4, so the arrow starts at v4, not the latest node v5.

q.q: How is a rollback shown on a version management graph?
o: Two arrows entering one node from parallel versions
An arrow pointing from a newer node back to an older one
A straight chain of nodes created one after another
A new node drawn from an older node, not the latest one
q.why: A rollback is shown by drawing the new version from an earlier node. Arrows never point backwards.

q.q: Which is one of the three conditions for version management to work successfully?
o: Only one developer may change the code files at any one time
Every developer keeps a personal copy of the files on their own laptop
Version numbers are only recorded for changes made to the main version
All team members use the same version of each code file when making changes
q.why: The three conditions: consistent tracking with version numbers, reversible changes, and everyone using the same version of each file.

q.q: A developer edits files directly on the server without committing them. Which condition is broken?
o: It is possible to reverse changes by rolling back to any earlier version
All team members use the same version of each code file when making changes
There is a consistent method of tracking changes, recording all version numbers
Every change is tested before it is merged into the main version of the code
q.why: Untracked changes bypass the system, so they have no version number and the history is incomplete.

q.q: A developer starts work from a copy of the code downloaded three weeks ago. Which condition for version management is most at risk?
o: It is possible to reverse changes
Changes are given a version number
Everyone uses the same version of each file
Commit notes are meaningful
q.why: Building on out-of-date code means their work will clash with everyone else's; retrieving the latest version first meets this condition.

q.q: Why should developers commit small changes regularly?
o: History stays detailed and merge conflicts stay small
It reduces the storage used by the repository
It means the code does not need to be tested
It hides unfinished work from the rest of the team
q.why: Small, frequent commits give a detailed history and keep conflicts small and easy to resolve.

q.q: Which condition for version management makes it possible to undo a faulty change?
o: It is possible to reverse changes
Everyone uses the same version of each file
Small changes are committed regularly
Each change has a meaningful note
q.why: Because any version can be retrieved, a faulty change can be undone by rolling back.

q.q: Which practice directly supports the condition that everyone works from the same version?
o: Writing meaningful commit notes for each change
Testing changes before merging them into main
Keeping a remote copy of the repository online
Retrieving the latest version before starting work
q.why: Retrieving the latest version first meets condition 3 and avoids building on old code.

q.q: What are CASE tools?
o: Programs that schedule meetings and messages for a remote development team
Hardware used to protect project files from loss if a computer fails
Programs that support or automate parts of the software development process
Standards that set out how a team names variables and lays out code
q.why: CASE (computer-aided software engineering) tools support or automate development stages.

q.q: Which is an example of an upper CASE tool?
o: A debugger for stepping through code
An automated testing tool
A code generator
A tool for drawing data flow diagrams
q.why: Upper CASE supports analysis and design, e.g. DFDs, ER diagrams, data dictionary, prototyping and project planning. The others are lower CASE.

q.q: What is the main purpose of integrated CASE?
o: To support only the analysis and design stages of the project life cycle
To automatically build and test the code every time a change is committed
To keep diagrams, data definitions and code consistent across the life cycle
To give a remote team messaging channels and video meetings for Scrums
q.why: Integrated CASE covers the whole life cycle and keeps diagrams, data definitions and code consistent.

q.q: Which is a drawback of CASE tools?
o: They cannot enforce any standard notation
Licences are expensive and staff need training
They prevent automatic code generation
They only check code, never designs
q.why: Drawbacks include expensive licences, the need for training and forcing a team into the tool's way of working.

q.q: A CASE tool warns that a data flow on a DFD has no source. Which benefit of CASE does this show?
o: Productivity
Collaboration
Quality
Elasticity
q.why: Checking designs for errors such as a data flow with no source is the quality benefit.

q.q: What does a continuous integration server do?
o: Automatically merges every branch into the main version each night
Holds the only copy of the specification, designs and user guides
Automatically builds and tests the code each time a change is committed
Shows who is working on what task and which tasks are blocked
q.why: CI builds and tests on each commit and reports failures to the team. Task boards show who is doing what.

q.q: A development team is spread across three offices. Which collaboration tool lets them see who is working on what and which tasks are blocked?
o: An issue tracker
A shared wiki
A task board
A code generator
q.why: Task boards show who is working on what and what is blocked. Shared wikis hold one up-to-date copy of documents.

q.q: What is a code review?
o: The client examines the finished system before it goes live
Other developers examine code before it is accepted into the main version
A tool automatically builds and tests the code after each commit
The tester runs the program against a test plan and logs defects
q.why: In a code review peers examine code, often via a pull request, before it is accepted.

q.q: Which is a benefit of code reviews?
o: They remove the need for any later testing of the system
Defects are found early and knowledge of the code is shared
They make the finished code run noticeably faster
They replace the need for a version management system
q.why: Reviews catch defects early, when cheapest to fix, and spread knowledge, reducing staff turnover risk.

q.q: Which practice is described in the notes as a continuous form of code review?
o: Continuous integration
Acceptance testing
Change control
Pair programming
q.why: Pair programming is a continuous form of review, since a second developer checks code as it is written.

q.q: What is the main difference between quality assurance and testing?
o: Testing covers the whole process; QA is one activity within it
QA covers the whole process; testing is one activity within it
QA is carried out only by the client once the system is finished
They are two names for the same activity at the end of a project
q.why: QA builds quality into every stage; testing is one QA activity, mainly on the product.

q.q: Which is an example of a coding standard?
o: The company follows ISO 9001 quality management
The website meets WCAG accessibility guidelines
All variables use meaningful camelCase names
Each objective has a single target value
q.why: Coding standards cover naming, indentation, commenting and error handling. ISO 9001 is a process standard; WCAG is a product standard.

q.q: WCAG accessibility guidelines are an example of which kind of standard?
o: Coding standard
Process standard
Product standard
Quality assurance standard
q.why: WCAG is the notes' example of a product standard, ensuring the product meets requirements such as access for users with disabilities.

q.q: Which is the main benefit of coding standards?
o: The client gains confidence in how the product is built
The product meets the needs of users with disabilities
The code needs no comments because names are short
Any developer can read and maintain anyone else's code
q.why: Coding standards make code consistent so any developer can read and maintain it. Client confidence is the process-standard benefit.

q.q: A function is written as: int f(int a){if(a>17)return 1;return 0;} Which coding standard problems does it show?
o: Too many comments and an over-long name
Unclear names, no comment and a magic number
A named constant used in place of a number
Meaningful names but inconsistent indenting
q.why: f and a say nothing, there is no comment, and 17 is a magic number. The improved version uses IsAdult, ageInYears and a named constant AdultAge.
